title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 10: recognising divine splendour in the world
excerpt: Original meanings and contextual explanations for all 42 verses on divine manifestations and the practice of recognition.
introHtml:
Arjuna asks how he can keep recognising Krishna while encountering a world of many things. Krishna responds with examples of vibhūti: distinctive manifestations of power, excellence and sustaining presence. The catalogue ranges through gods, sages, natural phenomena, language, human capacities and even unsettling forms of power. It is framed as a selection whose purpose is to direct attention toward the source that exceeds every list.

Each Meaning gives an original English rendering of the displayed Sanskrit. Each Explanation follows the verse’s wording, its place in the dialogue and its philosophical or devotional context. These are original reader explanations; named traditional interpretations are identified where they are compared. [1–3]

verses.meaningHtml: Krishna said: Hear once more my highest word, mighty-armed one. Because you listen with delight, I will speak to you with a desire for your welfare.
verses.explanationHtml: The renewed invitation treats Arjuna's listening as part of the relationship through which instruction continues. Krishna names concern for the listener's good as his motive, while acknowledging the delight the teaching has awakened. This opening prepares a chapter in which knowledge and devotion reinforce one another. The examples to come are intended to shape how Arjuna recognises the world and its source in continuing experience.

verses.meaningHtml: The hosts of gods and the great sages do not know my origin, for I am in every way the origin of the gods and the great sages.
verses.explanationHtml: Even beings associated with exceptional knowledge are situated within the dependence Krishna describes. Their inability to know his origin follows from his priority as their source. The claim extends beyond human limitations, giving theological force to the coming catalogue of divine and sage figures. Krishna's manifestations can be recognised among them while his reality remains prior to the existence and capacities of any particular member.

verses.meaningHtml: Whoever among mortals knows me as unborn, without beginning and the great Lord of the worlds is free from delusion and released from all wrongdoing.
verses.explanationHtml: The knowledge described here concerns the nature of Krishna's sourcehood. “Unborn” and “without beginning” distinguish him from a being whose origin would lie within the cosmic sequence he sustains. The verse gives this recognition a liberating consequence. It is therefore more than a classification of divine rank: the chapter presents understanding the world's dependence as something that changes the knower's orientation and relation to bondage.

verses.meaningHtml: Understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, patience, truthfulness, control of the senses, calm of mind, pleasure, pain, becoming, passing away, fear and fearlessness—
verses.explanationHtml: The sentence begins a list completed in the next verse. It includes cultivated virtues alongside conditions that living beings experience without simply choosing them. By placing understanding and self-control near pleasure, pain and fear, the text gives the account of divine sourcehood a broad scope. The list is not yet a set of instructions to adopt every condition named; its common predicate concerns their arising from Krishna.

verses.meaningHtml: Non-harming, equality, contentment, austerity, giving, honour and dishonour: these varied conditions of beings arise from me alone.
verses.explanationHtml: The concluding line supplies the claim governing both verses' lists. Many different capacities, dispositions and experiences depend upon the same divine source. Favourable and unfavourable conditions appear together, while the Gita elsewhere evaluates how people respond to them. That distinction matters for reading the catalogue: an account of what can arise within existence is broader than a catalogue of actions being recommended to the seeker.

verses.meaningHtml: The seven great sages, the four ancient ones, and the Manus, whose descendants are these people of the world, were born from my mind, endowed with my being.
verses.explanationHtml: The world's origin is described through its ancestral and sage lineages. The Sanskrit grouping has traditional interpretive differences: “the four ancient ones” can be connected with the Manus or understood as an additional group of primordial sages. The shared point is the dependence of these progenitors on Krishna's mind and power. The verse presents sacred genealogy as another way to contemplate the divine source of the living world. [3]

verses.meaningHtml: Whoever truly knows this manifestation and yoga of mine becomes joined through unwavering yoga. Of this there is no doubt.
verses.explanationHtml: Vibhūti and yoga together name the divine expression and the power through which it operates. Recognising them is said to steady the seeker's own yoga, giving the coming examples a practical purpose. They are aids to a settled understanding of dependence upon Krishna. The catalogue therefore belongs to the teaching about an integrated life of attention and devotion, rather than standing apart as an independent collection of remarkable names.

verses.meaningHtml: I am the origin of everything; everything proceeds from me. Understanding this, the wise worship me with a devoted disposition.
verses.explanationHtml: The relation between knowledge and worship is stated directly. The wise recognise Krishna as the source and continuing ground of all that proceeds, and that understanding takes the form of devotion. Bhāva gives the statement an affective depth: their recognition shapes the disposition with which they live. The verse thus explains why the chapter can move readily from claims about the world's origin to descriptions of loving religious practice.

verses.meaningHtml: With minds directed to me and lives devoted to me, enlightening one another and speaking continually of me, they find contentment and delight.
verses.explanationHtml: Devotion here includes a shared life of conversation and mutual understanding. The devotees are not described only as solitary contemplatives; they help one another recognise and discuss the object of their commitment. Satisfaction and delight are effects of that relationship. This also reflects the dialogue's own form, in which Arjuna's questions and Krishna's answers make sustained attention possible through speech between persons.

verses.meaningHtml: To those who are continually dedicated and worship me with love, I give the yoga of understanding through which they come to me.
verses.explanationHtml: Buddhi-yoga, introduced earlier as a discipline of understanding, is now described as a gift from Krishna to loving devotees. Their continued dedication and the divine response are presented together. The verse gives a personal account of how the understanding needed for attainment becomes available. It connects the seeker's practice with divine initiative, rather than treating insight as an achievement wholly detached from devotion.

verses.meaningHtml: Out of compassion for them, dwelling within their own being, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
verses.explanationHtml: The lamp image makes knowledge an illuminating presence within the devotee's life. Krishna speaks of destroying ignorance from within, giving the promised buddhi-yoga an intimate setting. Compassion supplies the motive for the action. The contrast of light and darkness is familiar to the chapter's coming examples, but here the concern is the person's understanding: the source of the world is also presented as the one who makes recognition possible.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the highest purifier, the eternal divine Person, the primordial deity, unborn and all-pervading—
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna begins an affirmation continued in the next verse. The titles gather up much of what Krishna has taught about imperishability, sourcehood and the highest goal. They also reveal how far the conversation has moved from the initial picture of a warrior addressing his charioteer. Arjuna is identifying the person before him with the comprehensive divine reality described in the teaching.

verses.meaningHtml: So all the sages proclaim you: the divine sage Narada, Asita, Devala and Vyasa. You yourself also tell me this.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna places Krishna's self-description beside the testimony of recognised sages. The named figures establish a setting of inherited religious authority, while the ongoing conversation supplies direct instruction. His affirmation does not end his questioning; the next verses turn it into a request for ways of contemplating what he has accepted. Trust in testimony and the wish for fuller understanding therefore remain connected within the dialogue.

verses.meaningHtml: I hold everything you tell me to be true, Keshava. Neither the gods nor the danavas know your manifestation, Lord.
verses.explanationHtml: The acknowledgement echoes Krishna's earlier statement about the limits of divine and sage knowledge. Arjuna accepts the instruction while recognising that the teacher's manifestation exceeds the grasp of powerful cosmic beings. This creates the basis for the request that follows: the one whose nature cannot be fully inferred from outside must explain how he can be recognised. The verse expresses trust together with an awareness of the scope of the inquiry.

verses.meaningHtml: You alone know yourself through yourself, highest Person, source of beings, Lord of beings, God of gods and Lord of the world.
verses.explanationHtml: The repeated addresses describe Krishna through the relationships already developed in the chapter. Source, lordship and supremacy over divine beings combine with the claim of self-knowledge. Arjuna's words acknowledge a limit to ordinary observation while asking the speaker to disclose himself. The point is significant to the narrative: the further teaching and the vision of Chapter 11 will arise through an act of divine self-revelation.

verses.meaningHtml: You should fully describe your divine manifestations, by which you pervade and remain throughout these worlds.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks for the many forms through which the comprehensive presence can be contemplated. The request concerns how Krishna pervades the worlds, giving concrete direction to the earlier abstract claims about sourcehood. “Fully” expresses the extent of Arjuna's desire to hear, while Krishna will soon clarify that any spoken list must be selective. The tension between inexhaustible reality and finite description shapes the chapter's catalogue.

verses.meaningHtml: How may I know you, yogin, by continually contemplating you? In which particular conditions or forms should I think of you, Lord?
verses.explanationHtml: The practical question is one of sustained recognition. Arjuna wants points of attention through which remembrance can continue amid particular experiences. His request gives the examples their pedagogical function: an exceptional manifestation can direct the mind toward the divine presence on which it depends. The catalogue that follows is therefore connected with the everyday discipline of contemplation, even when some of its examples belong to the cosmic or mythic world.

verses.meaningHtml: Tell me again in detail of your yoga and manifestation, Janardana, for I find no satiation in hearing your nectar-like words.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna's eagerness gives an affective setting to his request for knowledge. The imagery of nectar describes the sustaining delight of listening, while the desire for detail keeps inquiry active. The chapter began with Krishna recognising this delight, and Arjuna now confirms it in his own speech. The exchange makes understanding, trust and enjoyment of the teaching mutually reinforcing parts of the developing devotional relationship.

verses.meaningHtml: Krishna said: Yes, I shall describe to you my divine manifestations in their chief examples, best of the Kurus, for there is no end to my extent.
verses.explanationHtml: The answer sets the method and the limit of what follows. The examples are principal manifestations, not an exhaustive enclosure of divine reality within a list. This framing prevents the reader from treating the named things as the only places where Krishna can be recognised. The concluding verses will repeat the point and provide a general way of extending the contemplation beyond the examples explicitly supplied.

verses.meaningHtml: I am the self dwelling in the hearts of all beings, Gudakesha. I am their beginning, their middle and also their end.
verses.explanationHtml: The first manifestation is inward and universal. Krishna is identified with the self present in all beings and with the entire course of their existence. This opening gives a foundation for the more differentiated examples: they are considered within a reality that already concerns every being. The language of heart or inner dwelling also connects the cosmic catalogue with the personal illumination described in verse 10.11.

verses.meaningHtml: Among the Adityas I am Vishnu; among lights, the radiant sun. Among the Maruts I am Marichi, and among the lunar mansions or stars, the moon.
verses.explanationHtml: The examples move through groups of divine and celestial powers. Each group is given a distinguished manifestation through which Krishna can be contemplated. Nakṣatra belongs to the traditional language of the starry and lunar sky, so the moon's place in the list follows that setting. The structure teaches attention through prominence and luminosity while keeping each manifestation related to the larger source announced at the chapter's opening.

verses.meaningHtml: Among the Vedas I am the Sama Veda; among the gods, Vasava, Indra. Among the senses I am mind, and among living beings I am consciousness.
verses.explanationHtml: Sacred song, divine sovereignty, coordination of the senses and living awareness are placed beside one another. The Sama Veda gives a ritual and musical form to sacred utterance, while mind gathers the senses' activity into experience. Consciousness then names a pervasive feature of living beings. The sequence broadens the field of recognition, showing that the teaching moves through both highly distinguished figures and functions present within ordinary embodied life.

verses.meaningHtml: Among the Rudras I am Shankara; among yakshas and rakshasas, the lord of wealth. Among the Vasus I am fire, and among mountains with peaks, Meru.
verses.explanationHtml: Divine groups, guardianship of wealth, elemental fire and the cosmic mountain supply the next comparisons. The lord of wealth is the figure commonly called Kubera in this setting, while Shankara names Shiva among the Rudras. The point of the verse is the selection of a commanding or distinctive presence within each class. Its cosmological and religious references give the contemplative practice a recognisable cultural world.

verses.meaningHtml: Among household priests, know me as the chief, Brihaspati, Partha. Among army commanders I am Skanda; among bodies of water I am the ocean.
verses.explanationHtml: Priestly guidance and military leadership connect the catalogue with two forms of authority important in the epic. The ocean then supplies an image of natural vastness. Brihaspati and Skanda are named within their traditional divine roles, allowing the listener to contemplate knowledge, command and immensity through specific examples. The verse's movement across these domains reinforces the breadth of the manifestations rather than limiting recognition to one kind of excellence.

verses.meaningHtml: Among the great sages I am Bhrigu; among utterances, the single syllable Om. Among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of recitation; among immovable things, the Himalaya.
verses.explanationHtml: The sequence links a sage, a concentrated sacred sound, a repeated devotional act and a mountain range. Japa-yajña places recitation within the language of sacrifice, connecting an accessible practice with the larger ritual framework. Om condenses sacred utterance into one syllable, while the Himalaya expresses enduring grandeur through place. The examples give contemplation both inwardly repeatable and outwardly recognisable supports.

verses.meaningHtml: Among all trees I am the ashvattha; among divine sages, Narada. Among gandharvas I am Chitraratha; among perfected beings, the sage Kapila.
verses.explanationHtml: A tree and three distinguished figures bring together sacred landscape, seership, celestial artistry and perfected knowledge. The ashvattha, familiar as the pipal tree, will become the central image of Chapter 15 in a different context. Here it is one selected manifestation among trees. The verse's named examples retain their particular identities while serving the shared purpose of directing attention toward Krishna through what is especially honoured or accomplished.

verses.meaningHtml: Among horses, know me as Ucchaihshravas, born with the nectar of immortality; among lordly elephants, Airavata; and among people, the king.
verses.explanationHtml: The first two examples come from the traditional narrative of the churning for nectar, which explains the phrase “born with immortality's nectar.” The royal example then brings the sequence into human social order. The verse selects figures of exceptional stature within their classes, continuing the chapter's contemplative method. Its recognition of a king's prominence belongs to that method and its epic setting, rather than settling the conduct of every individual ruler.

verses.meaningHtml: Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows, the wish-fulfilling cow. I am Kandarpa, the power of generation, and among serpents I am Vasuki.
verses.explanationHtml: Force, abundance, generation and serpent sovereignty provide distinct forms of power. The thunderbolt carries martial force, the wish-fulfilling cow expresses sustaining plenty, and Kandarpa names desire in its generative aspect. This last example recalls the qualified recognition of desire in verse 7.11. The verse works through the religious and mythic associations of its examples, placing their characteristic capacities within Krishna's account of divine manifestation.

verses.meaningHtml: Among nagas I am Ananta; among beings of the waters, Varuna. Among ancestors I am Aryaman; among those who restrain, I am Yama.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse moves through serpent, aquatic, ancestral and regulative domains. Its distinction between the serpent categories in this and the previous verse follows the inherited classification rather than a modern zoological scheme. Varuna, Aryaman and Yama connect cosmic order with the bonds and limits of living existence. The examples make support, ancestral relationship and restraint further points through which the divine presence can be contemplated.

verses.meaningHtml: Among the daityas I am Prahlada; among those who reckon, I am time. Among animals I am the lion, and among birds, the son of Vinata.
verses.explanationHtml: Prahlada places a distinguished devotee within the daitya lineage, complicating any assumption that the catalogue merely follows a single group's social or cosmic prestige. Time then names the measure within which reckoning occurs. The lion and Vinata's son, Garuda, supply powerful animal and bird examples. Together they continue to expand the kinds of prominence through which recognition is possible, including devotion, measurement, strength and mythic sovereignty.

verses.meaningHtml: Among purifiers I am the wind; among bearers of weapons, Rama. Among creatures of the waters I am the makara, and among streams I am Jahnavi, the Ganga.
verses.explanationHtml: Purifying movement, armed excellence, an imposing aquatic creature and a sacred river form the next sequence. The makara belongs to the text's traditional aquatic imagery; its exact identification need not be reduced to one modern animal species for the verse's purpose. Jahnavi names the Ganga through its inherited story and sacred identity. These examples connect the contemplative practice with motion, protection, water and familiar religious geography.

verses.meaningHtml: Of creations I am the beginning, the end and the middle, Arjuna. Among fields of knowledge I am knowledge of the self; among those who debate, I am reasoned discussion.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse returns to the entire course of existence, then identifies two forms of understanding. Adhyātma-vidyā gives knowledge of the self a central place, consistent with the Gita's inquiry into action and liberation. Vāda points toward reasoned discussion aimed at establishing what is true. Its presence in the catalogue gives reflective exchange, including the dialogue itself, a place among the manifestations of divine excellence.

verses.meaningHtml: Among letters I am the sound A; among compounds, the coordinate compound. I am inexhaustible time, and the sustainer whose faces are everywhere.
verses.explanationHtml: Language becomes a field of contemplation through its elementary sound and its forms of combination. The coordinate compound, dvandva, joins terms while preserving their paired or grouped standing. The verse then moves from linguistic structure to inexhaustible time and all-facing support. The range is deliberate: both the articulation of speech and the encompassing conditions of existence can direct thought toward the sustaining presence Krishna describes.

verses.meaningHtml: I am death, which takes everything away, and the arising of those yet to be. Among feminine powers I am fame, prosperity, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness and forgiveness.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse names both the removal of existing forms and the emergence of new ones. It then turns to a group of qualities expressed in feminine terms, with resonances of their personified divine forms. The list includes capacities of speech, memory and judgement alongside patience and forgiveness. Its placement gives birth, loss and cultivated excellence a shared setting within the chapter's account of the powers sustaining and transforming the world.

verses.meaningHtml: Among Sama chants I am the Brihat Saman; among metres, Gayatri. Among months I am Margashirsha, and among seasons, the flower-bearing spring.
verses.explanationHtml: Particular forms of sacred sound and particular divisions of the year are selected for contemplation. The Brihat Saman and Gayatri concern the organisation of recitation, while Margashirsha and the flowering season locate excellence within recurrent time. The verse encourages recognition through features of religious and seasonal life that listeners can encounter repeatedly. Its specificity is part of its usefulness: remembrance is given concrete occasions rather than remaining only a general abstraction.

verses.meaningHtml: Among deceivers I am gambling; I am the brilliance of the brilliant. I am victory, resolve and the goodness or strength of those endowed with it.
verses.explanationHtml: Gambling is an intentionally unsettling example within a catalogue otherwise easy to associate with admired qualities. It identifies a commanding power within deception, broadening the account of manifestation beyond a simple list of moral recommendations. Victory and resolve then name forceful human capacities, while sattva carries senses of goodness, vigour and steadiness. The surrounding teaching still evaluates conduct; recognising dependence upon a source does not remove those distinctions.

verses.meaningHtml: Among the Vrishnis I am Vasudeva; among the Pandavas, Dhananjaya. Among sages I am Vyasa; among inspired poets, Ushanas.
verses.explanationHtml: The catalogue enters the immediate world of the speakers. Vasudeva names Krishna himself, and Dhananjaya names Arjuna, the listener receiving the teaching. The exemplars are therefore not confined to distant mythic or cosmic domains. Vyasa and Ushanas add forms of seership and inspired speech, bringing the production and transmission of understanding into view. Arjuna can recognise his own capacity within the larger dependence Krishna has described.

verses.meaningHtml: Among those who discipline I am the rod of authority; among those seeking victory, sound policy. Among secrets I am silence, and among knowers, knowledge.
verses.explanationHtml: The examples concern how power and understanding are exercised. Discipline and strategy connect the verse with governance, while silence gives secrecy its effective form. Knowledge finally identifies the distinguishing capacity of the knower. The varied sequence invites attention to what makes an activity effective or a role meaningful. Within the chapter, those enabling powers become occasions for contemplating their divine ground and their place in an integrated life.

verses.meaningHtml: Whatever is the seed of all beings, I am that, Arjuna. No moving or unmoving being exists that could be without me.
verses.explanationHtml: The seed image returns from Chapter 7 to summarise a universal dependence. The many exceptional examples have not replaced the claim concerning every being. Moving and unmoving together express that breadth, while “without me” states its ontological force. This verse gives the catalogue its foundation: distinguished manifestations are useful points of recognition because the whole field of existence already depends upon the reality they help disclose.

verses.meaningHtml: There is no end to my divine manifestations, scorcher of foes. This account of their extent has been given only by way of indication.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna repeats the limitation with which he introduced the examples. The list points toward an inexhaustible reality and cannot fully enumerate it. This matters for the reader's use of the chapter: the exercise is to learn a manner of recognition that can continue beyond the named cases. The following verse supplies a general principle for making that extension while preserving the relation between a manifestation and its source.

verses.meaningHtml: Whatever being has distinctive splendour, beauty or force, understand that very thing to arise from a portion of my radiance.
verses.explanationHtml: The selection of examples becomes a broader rule of contemplation. Splendour, prosperity and vigorous power can direct attention toward the radiance from which they arise. Aṃśa, “portion,” gives the relation a language of participation without turning any single example into an exhaustive measure of Krishna. The claim also keeps the world's real distinctions of capacity visible: their prominence can serve recognition while their dependence remains fundamental.

verses.meaningHtml: Or what need have you of knowing all this in detail, Arjuna? Supporting this whole world with a single portion of myself, I remain.
verses.explanationHtml: The conclusion gathers the catalogue into one comprehensive statement. Krishna's sustaining presence exceeds the sum of the examples, and even the world as a whole is described through only a portion of his power. The question redirects attention from accumulating names to understanding that dependence. It also prepares Arjuna's next request: having heard the comprehensive claim, he will ask to see the divine form in which the world is held together.
